{"id": "3215309d-5ea7-4b8a-a9eb-5cdf6e9e7128", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "A customer published 412.7 MTCO2e (location-based, TOTAL_LBM_CARBON_EMISSIONS) as its FY2025 AWS footprint, covering January to December 2025, taken from the AWS Sustainability console when an earlier carbon model version was current. Today GetEstimatedCarbonEmissions for the same twelve months returns a location-based total of 468.3 MTCO2e, with ModelVersion v3.0.1 on every month. The customer did no optimization work. They ask: 'Why does AWS now show a different number for the same year? Did our footprint regress? And can you pull the figure under the old model so we can compare?' Answer using the skill's guidance. No AWS access required.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "4884ec00-945b-4f58-bb4b-43990604a793", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_2YZz4C7xgPuZEhHLJ9MeMZ", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"---\\\\nname: sustainability-operation-review\\\\ndescription: Workload sustainability review aligned with the AWS Well-Architected\\\\n  Sustainability Pillar (SUS01-SUS06), combining carbon emissions and water\\\\n  withdrawal data from the AWS Sustainability API with topology-derived resource\\\\n  intensity KPIs. Use this skill when a user asks to review or audit a workload\\'s\\\\n  sustainability posture, carbon footprint, emissions, water usage, environmental\\\\n  impact, or resource efficiency. Activate on requests like \\\\\"sustainability\\\\n  review\\\\\", \\\\\"carbon footprint analysis\\\\\", \\\\\"Well-Architected sustainability\\\\n  assessment\\\\\", \\\\\"why did my emissions increase\\\\\", \\\\\"reduce our carbon footprint\\\\\",\\\\n  \\\\\"sustainability KPIs\\\\\", \\\\\"green IT review\\\\\", or \\\\\"SUS pillar audit\\\\\". Also activate\\\\n  when emissions rose despite optimization work, when a user asks for emissions by\\\\n  linked account, service or Region, or about Graviton for sustainability, attaches\\\\n  a carbon or water CSV export from the AWS Sustainability console, or asks\\\\n  about AI/ML workloads on Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock, or GPU,\\\\n  Inferentia or Trainium instances.\\\\nmetadata:\\\\n  author: rrrazvan\\\\n  version: \\\\\"1.0.0\\\\\"\\\\n  summary: \\\\\"Well-Architected Sustainability review: resource-intensity KPIs as the assessment, carbon emissions as context, plus Graviton and AI/ML checks.\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: \\\\\"CHAT, PREVENTION\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: \\\\\"AWS Sustainability, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon RDS, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: \\\\\"Sustainability, Cost Optimization\\\\\"\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Workload Sustainability Review\\\\n\\\\nReview a workload against the 29 best practices of the\\\\n[AWS Well-Architected Sustainability Pillar](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/sustainability-pillar/sustainability-pillar.html).\\\\nResource intensity KPIs derived from the topology are the assessment; emissions from the\\\\n[AWS Sustainability API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sustainability/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html)\\\\nare context.\\\\n\\\\n## \\\\u26a0\\\\ufe0f Critical \\\\u2014 read first\\\\n\\\\n- **Load each named file in full, at the step that names it**, with `read_skill_resource`.\\\\n  Never `distill` or summarize this skill or its files in their place, and never grade from memory.\\\\n- **If a load fails, say so.** Start the report with `\\\\u26a0\\\\ufe0f <file> could not be loaded: <verbatim\\\\n  error>`, do not replace its rules with general knowledge, and mark the practices that depend\\\\n  on it NEEDS HUMAN INPUT.\\\\n- **Emissions are context; resource intensity KPIs are the assessment.** Never attribute a\\\\n  change in reported emissions to a customer action, and never state a recommendation\\'s impact\\\\n  in MTCO2e. Use vCPU-hours, weighted GB-months, GB transferred, accelerator-hours or tokens.\\\\n- **Never estimate CO2e** for a Graviton migration, AI/ML workload, token, inference or training\\\\n  run. Quote AWS\\'s Graviton energy statement only as AWS\\'s.\\\\n- **Sanity-check emissions against the topology** (Step 6). Zero or near-zero emissions next\\\\n  to a sizeable fleet, or emissions shares that don\\'t match where the resources are, mean the\\\\n  two inputs cover different scopes. Report that as a finding; never explain it away.\\\\n- **Only a service-returned `AccessDeniedException` is a permissions gap**; name the missing\\\\n  action. For any other failure, record the message verbatim, recommend no IAM change, and\\\\n  name no permission, not even as a conditional.\\\\n- **Absent or zero emissions are below the reporting threshold** (0.5 g CO2e, 0.5 mL water),\\\\n  not zero impact. Carbon for month M publishes by the 21st of M+1, so before the 21st the\\\\n  latest month can be two back. That is the normal one-month lag, not missing data.\\\\n- **Never invent a business output metric.** Use the Step 1 fallback and say which.\\\\n- **Grade all 29 practices.** Never mark one MET without evidence; use NEEDS HUMAN INPUT.\\\\n- **Read-only.** Never call `Modify*`, `Delete*`, `Terminate*` or `Create*`. Every\\\\n  recommendation is for a human to action.\\\\n- **Never call efficiency work immaterial.** Provisioning decides how much AWS infrastructure\\\\n  is allocated to the account; rightsizing and decommissioning reduce it.\\\\n- **Compare months per day.** A 28-day month carries about 10% less than a 31-day one at the\\\\n  same usage; a delta smaller than the day-count difference is not a finding.\\\\n- **Always finish.** Produce the full report even when emissions data is unavailable.\\\\n- **The report artifact is the deliverable.** Create it with [assets/report-template.md](assets/report-template.md) at\\\\n  Step 9 even when the user asks specific questions; answer them in its Executive Summary, then\\\\n  summarize in chat.\\\\n- **Keep Steps 7\\\\u20139 in this conversation.** If you delegate data collection, still load the\\\\n  checklist and the template yourself, grade all 29 practices, and write the report here.\\\\n\\\\n## When to use\\\\n\\\\nFor architecture-level sustainability reviews. Not for per-instance rightsizing (point to\\\\n[AWS Compute Optimizer](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/compute-optimizer/latest/ug/what-is-compute-optimizer.html)),\\\\ncost reduction as the main goal, or incident-time analysis: there is no live carbon signal.\\\\n\\\\n## Workflow checklist\\\\n\\\\n- [ ] Step 1: Scope and business output metric\\\\n- [ ] Step 2: Topology \\\\u2014 load [references/workload-model.md](references/workload-model.md)\\\\n- [ ] Step 3: Workload shape and triggers\\\\n- [ ] Step 4: Resource intensity inputs \\\\u2014 load [references/proxy-metrics.md](references/proxy-metrics.md)\\\\n- [ ] Step 5: Environmental impact data \\\\u2014 load [references/framing-and-attribution.md](references/framing-and-attribution.md),\\\\n  [references/emissions-collection.md](references/emissions-collection.md) and [references/emissions-api-reference.md](references/emissions-api-reference.md)\\\\n- [ ] Step 6: KPIs, emissions sanity check, cost\\\\u2013carbon divergence\\\\n- [ ] Step 7: Assess all 29 practices \\\\u2014 load [references/sus-best-practices-checklist.md](references/sus-best-practices-checklist.md)\\\\n- [ ] Step 8: Explain emissions changes\\\\n- [ ] Step 9: Report \\\\u2014 load [assets/report-template.md](assets/report-template.md)\\\\n\\\\nDo not start a step before the previous one is done. Do not start Step 7 or Step 9 until its\\\\nfile is loaded.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1 \\\\u2014 Scope and business output metric\\\\n\\\\nAsk for the scope (an entry point, application, set of accounts, or \\\\\"everything in this\\\\naccount\\\\\"; default: all configured Regions) and the business output metric \\\\u2014 the unit of work\\\\nthe workload produces. It is the denominator of every intensity KPI. If there is none, use the\\\\nfirst available fallback and state its caveat:\\\\n\\\\n1. Request count \\\\u2014 ALB `RequestCount`, API Gateway `Count`, CloudFront `Requests`\\\\n2. Invocation count \\\\u2014 Lambda `Invocations`, SQS `NumberOfMessagesDeleted`\\\\n3. Data processed \\\\u2014 S3 `BytesDownloaded`, Kinesis `IncomingRecords`\\\\n4. None \\\\u2014 report absolute footprint only, and make SUS06-BP01 the top recommendation\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2 \\\\u2014 Topology\\\\n\\\\nLoad [references/workload-model.md](references/workload-model.md). Walk the Agent Space topology from the entry point,\\\\nclassify every resource into a layer, and record each resource\\'s Region. Fill gaps with\\\\n`tag:GetResources` and service `Describe*` calls, and state any coverage gap.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3 \\\\u2014 Shape and triggers\\\\n\\\\nDetect the workload shape with the table in `workload-model.md` and state the evidence.\\\\n- ML / accelerated shape, or `Invocations` in the `AWS/Bedrock` namespace \\\\u2192 load\\\\n  [references/ai-ml-workloads.md](references/ai-ml-workloads.md).\\\\n- Any x86 compute or managed instance class \\\\u2192 load [references/graviton-migration.md](references/graviton-migration.md).\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4 \\\\u2014 Resource intensity inputs\\\\n\\\\nLoad [references/proxy-metrics.md](references/proxy-metrics.md). Over 30 days at `Period: 3600`, derive provisioned and\\\\nutilized vCPU-hours (vCPU \\\\u00d7 hours \\\\u00d7 utilization, never instance counts), weighted GB-months\\\\nand weighted GB transferred, and the business output for the same window. Record each\\\\nresource\\'s architecture (`x86_64` or `arm64`) and instance generation. The storage and\\\\nnetwork weights are directional, not a carbon model; say so in the report. For AI/ML, collect\\\\nthe inputs listed in `ai-ml-workloads.md`.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 5 \\\\u2014 Environmental impact data\\\\n\\\\nLoad [references/framing-and-attribution.md](references/framing-and-attribution.md) and [references/emissions-collection.md](references/emissions-collection.md), and\\\\nread [references/emissions-api-reference.md](references/emissions-api-reference.md) before the first call. If a carbon or water `.csv`\\\\nexport is attached, or the customer prefers to supply one instead of granting API access, load\\\\n[references/csv-emissions-input.md](references/csv-emissions-input.md) first; an attached export wins over the API for its metric.\\\\n- Carbon: `GetEstimatedCarbonEmissions`, 14 months, `MONTHLY`, paginated \\\\u2014 one call grouped by\\\\n  `SERVICE` and `REGION`, one by `USAGE_ACCOUNT_ID`. More than one account returned is a\\\\n  management-account view: report per account and say so. Only this account is a member or\\\\n  standalone view. Never assert either without that evidence. Only EC2, S3 and CloudFront are\\\\n  broken out by service; the rest is \\\\\"Other\\\\\". `GetEstimatedCarbonEmissionsDimensionValues` is\\\\n  optional; if it fails, continue.\\\\n- Water: `GetEstimatedWaterAllocation`, `YEARLY_CALENDAR`, `Start` on 1 January. Whatever the\\\\n  source, API or export, always state: m3, annual only, water **withdrawn (not consumed)**, AWS\\\\n  data-center operations only, excluding water embodied in upstream electricity. It is\\\\n  disclosure only: no Well-Architected practice or KPI is water-specific, so derive no finding,\\\\n  KPI, trend driver or recommendation from it, and never attribute a change in it to the\\\\n  customer. If asked how to reduce it, say in one sentence that the review\\'s resource-efficiency\\\\n  findings are the only levers; list no water actions.\\\\n  If the call fails or returns nothing, ask for a water export from the Sustainability console\\\\n  and load [references/csv-emissions-input.md](references/csv-emissions-input.md).\\\\n- Attempt carbon and water independently, record the `ModelVersion`, and handle every failure\\\\n  with the \\\\\"no data\\\\\" table in `emissions-collection.md`.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 6 \\\\u2014 KPIs and checks\\\\n\\\\nUse the KPI set in `proxy-metrics.md` that fits the shape: current value, 30 days prior,\\\\nchange, direction. Add the Graviton KPIs from `graviton-migration.md`, and report AI/ML KPIs\\\\nfrom `ai-ml-workloads.md` in a separate table. Then:\\\\n- **Emissions sanity check** \\\\u2014 compare emissions with the provisioned footprint using the\\\\n  tests in `proxy-metrics.md`. If one fails, report the scope mismatch as a finding.\\\\n- **Cost vs carbon divergence** \\\\u2014 `ce:GetCostAndUsage` over the same window; test the five\\\\n  patterns in `proxy-metrics.md`. On `AccessDeniedException`, skip and say so. If none applies,\\\\n  say so plainly.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 7 \\\\u2014 Assess all 29 practices\\\\n\\\\nLoad [references/sus-best-practices-checklist.md](references/sus-best-practices-checklist.md). For every practice, apply its evidence,\\\\nNOT MET / PARTIAL criteria, severity and guard, and record status and evidence. Use\\\\n`graviton-migration.md` for SUS05-BP02 and the lens mapping in `ai-ml-workloads.md`, citing the\\\\nlens ID after the SUS ID, as in `SUS05-BP04 (MLSUS05-BP02)`. Never recommend a Region move\\\\nwithout confirmed residency, latency and service availability; report SUS05-BP01 at fleet\\\\nlevel only. Severity, from most to least urgent: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, INFO. It reflects\\\\nresource-footprint impact and remediation effort, not operational risk; definitions are in\\\\n[assets/report-template.md](assets/report-template.md).\\\\n\\\\n### Step 8 \\\\u2014 Explain emissions changes\\\\n\\\\nIf reported emissions changed, work through the ordered causes in\\\\n`framing-and-attribution.md` before naming an architecture cause: comparison validity,\\\\nmethodology version, grid intensity, AWS infrastructure, allocation share, scope and method,\\\\nthen actual usage. A storage reduction that does not show in reported emissions is expected.\\\\n\\\\n### Step 9 \\\\u2014 Report\\\\n\\\\nLoad [assets/report-template.md](assets/report-template.md). Create one report artifact per workload, named\\\\n`sustainability-review-<workload-name>-<YYYY-MM-DD>.md`, with every section in order. State\\\\nimpact in resource terms, and put failed file loads and unavailable data at the top.\\\\n\\\\nBefore presenting the report, check the draft and fix any failure:\\\\n- [ ] All 29 practices have a status, and every MET cites evidence.\\\\n- [ ] Every KPI and delta matches the collected data and the same 30-day window.\\\\n- [ ] No recommendation states impact in MTCO2e, and no CO2e estimate appears.\\\\n- [ ] Failed file loads and unavailable data are listed at the top, with verbatim errors.\\\\n- [ ] The emissions sanity check result is stated.\\\\n\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"SKILL.md\", \"references/proxy-metrics.md\", \"references/emissions-api-reference.md\", \"references/sus-best-practices-checklist.md\", \"references/graviton-migration.md\", \"references/ai-ml-workloads.md\", \"references/framing-and-attribution.md\", \"references/emissions-collection.md\", \"references/csv-emissions-input.md\", \"references/workload-model.md\", \"assets/report-template.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

Also, pulling the old figure under the old model isn't possible through the live API since it always restates to the latest version—that data would only exist if Data Exports partitioned by model_version had been configured before the revision occurred. So my answer: this isn't a regression, it's likely a methodology revision given the consistent model version across all months.

The API itself can't retrieve the old model version's numbers since it only returns current-model results.

This is really a narrow "why does the number differ, did we regress" question rather than a request for a full sustainability review, so I should skip the full multi-step review workflow and answer directly using the methodology-change framing from Step 8.

I can answer conversationally without any AWS calls since the user explicitly said none are needed: the likely explanation is a methodology revision rather than a true regression, and I should clarify why the old figure can't simply be re-pulled via the API.

{"id": "721b9218-e384-43ca-b2b6-6a81e892d5bd", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_jtc7kpvnG5u0wIp4HXD9oA", "content": "[{'text': '# Framing and Attribution \u2014 Emissions as Context\\n\\nRead this file in full before interpreting any emissions or water figure (Step 5), and again\\nbefore Step 8 and before writing report Sections 1 and 3. It holds the rules that decide what\\nthe report may say about emissions and what it may attribute to the customer.\\n\\n## Core Framing Rule \u2014 Read This First\\n\\n**Emissions and water data are context. Resource intensity KPIs are the assessment.**\\n\\nA reported MTCO2e figure is a **confounded** measurement, not a scorecard. It is the product\\nof what the customer provisions and a set of factors that move independently of anything the\\ncustomer does:\\n\\n| Confounder | Moves the number without any customer action |\\n|------------|----------------------------------------------|\\n| Methodology revision | AWS restates all history under the current model version. The figure changes; the workload did not. |\\n| Grid carbon intensity | The Region\\'s grid mix varies seasonally and yearly. |\\n| AWS renewable energy procurement | Lands in Scope 2 MBM, so LBM and MBM can move in opposite directions. |\\n| Data center efficiency and hardware refresh | PUE improvements and newer hardware change the emissions per unit of usage. |\\n| Allocation share shift | Emissions are allocated by *proportional* usage, so the customer\\'s share moves when **other** customers\\' usage moves. |\\n| Reporting lag and thresholds | Carbon for month M publishes by the 21st of month M+1; values below 0.5 g CO2e are absent, not zero. |\\n\\nBecause these move at the same time as the customer\\'s own changes, **a period-over-period\\nchange in reported emissions cannot be attributed to a customer action without first ruling\\nthem out** (Step 8). That is a statement about attribution, not about magnitude: customer\\ndecisions can and do move the reported figure substantially \u2014 provisioning determines how much\\nAWS infrastructure gets allocated to the account in the first place, and Region choice is an\\nexplicit Pillar best practice (SUS01-BP01). The problem is that the emissions figure alone\\ncannot tell you *which* cause was responsible.\\n\\nResource intensity KPIs have no such confounders: they measure what the customer provisioned\\nand used, directly. That is why they are the assessment and emissions are the context.\\n\\n**Water withdrawal is allocated by the same top-down method and carries the same\\nconfounders** \u2014 treat it identically to carbon throughout.\\n\\nNote what this does **not** mean. It does not mean efficiency work is futile or that the\\ncustomer\\'s slice is too small to matter. The division of responsibility is that AWS owns the\\n*efficiency of the infrastructure* (PUE, renewable supply, hardware) while the customer owns\\n*how much of it they consume* \u2014 and that second quantity is what every recommendation in this\\nskill targets. Never tell a customer their rightsizing or decommissioning work is immaterial\\nto their footprint; embodied hardware carbon in particular scales with what they provision.\\n\\nYou MUST NOT claim causality between a customer action and a change in reported\\nemissions. Specifically:\\n\\n| Never say | Say instead |\\n|-----------|-------------|\\n| \"Your optimization reduced emissions by X MTCO2e\" | \"Reported emissions fell X MTCO2e over this period. Grid intensity and AWS infrastructure changes also moved in this window, so this figure cannot be attributed to the architecture change. The resource intensity KPI fell Y%, which *is* attributable.\" |\\n| \"Emissions increased, so the workload regressed\" | \"Reported emissions increased. Check the methodology version and grid intensity first \u2014 see Step 8 before treating this as a regression.\" |\\n| \"This change will save X MTCO2e\" | \"This change reduces provisioned vCPU-hours by X%, which reduces the resource footprint the emissions model allocates to you.\" |\\n| \"Moving to Graviton will cut your emissions by 60%\" | \"AWS states that Graviton-based EC2 instances use up to 60% less energy than comparable EC2 instances for the same performance. This review does not estimate the effect on your reported emissions. The migration moves X vCPU-hours/month to Graviton, which you can track through compute intensity.\" |\\n\\nResource intensity KPIs *are* attributable to customer action, because they measure\\nwhat the customer provisions and consumes. Lead with them.\\n\\n## Step 8: Explain Emissions Changes Before Attributing Them\\n\\nIf reported emissions changed period-over-period, work through these causes **in this\\norder** before considering an architecture change as the explanation:\\n\\n0. **Is the comparison even valid?** Only when the data came from a CSV (Step 5.0). An\\n   incomplete latest period, two different `model_version` values, or a period length\\n   mismatch will each manufacture an apparent change out of nothing. If any of these applies,\\n   there is no change to explain \u2014 report the coverage and stop here.\\n1. **Methodology version change** \u2014 a revision can move reported figures substantially with\\n   zero change in usage. History is restated under the current model, so all months in a\\n   response share one `ModelVersion` and you **cannot** detect a revision by comparing\\n   periods. Instead compare it against the version behind any figure the customer published\\n   previously; if it differs, their earlier number was restated \u2014 the change is in the\\n   instrument, not the workload. Say so and stop here. Carbon and water version\\n   independently, so check the relevant one.\\n2. **Grid carbon intensity** \u2014 the Region\\'s grid mix changes seasonally and yearly.\\n   Emissions can rise while usage falls, or fall with no customer action.\\n3. **AWS-side infrastructure changes** \u2014 hardware refresh, PUE improvements, and\\n   renewable energy procurement all move the number without customer action.\\n4. **Allocation share shift** \u2014 CCFT allocates a share of AWS infrastructure emissions\\n   based on proportional usage. Your share can change because *other* customers\\' usage\\n   changed.\\n5. **Scope composition** \u2014 check whether the change is in Scope 1, 2, or 3, and in LBM vs\\n   MBM. Scope 2 MBM is where AWS renewable purchases land, so LBM and MBM often move in\\n   opposite directions and a customer reading the wrong series draws the wrong conclusion.\\n6. **Actual usage change** \u2014 after ruling out 1\u20135, correlate against the resource intensity\\n   KPIs from Step 6. This is a legitimate and often substantial cause, not a leftover:\\n   provisioned capacity drives the allocation, and embodied hardware carbon (frequently the\\n   largest scope) scales with it. If the KPIs moved in the same direction and the confounders\\n   above are ruled out, say the usage change is the **most likely** explanation \u2014 while still\\n   not asserting a precise causal split, because the confounders were ruled out, not measured.\\n\\nThe ordering exists because the confounders are invisible in the figure itself, so they must be\\neliminated first. It does **not** rank them by size, and reaching step 6 is a normal outcome.\\n\\nA storage reduction that does not show up as an emissions reduction is the **expected**\\nresult, not an anomaly. Say so directly \u2014 customers who have done real optimization work and\\nsee no movement in reported emissions need this explained, not hedged. Always read the `TimePeriod` on each returned result rather than\\ninferring which months the request covered.\\n\\nReturned results use the same half-open representation \u2014 a January result carries\\n`Start: 2025-01-01T00:00:00Z, End: 2025-02-01T00:00:00Z`.\\n\\n### 2. Absent \u2260 zero\\n\\nImpact below 0.5 g CO2e (0.0000005 MTCO2e) is not reported. Neither is data for an\\naccount too new to have published data. Both appear as absence. Distinguish:\\n- \"No data available for this period (publication lag)\"\\n- \"Impact below the reporting threshold\"\\n- \"Zero measured impact\"\\n\\n### 4. Organization scope depends on the calling identity\\n\\n- **Management account** \u2192 consolidated data for all member accounts, for the periods\\n  those accounts were in the organization. Membership changes therefore shift history.\\n- **Member account** \u2192 its own data only.\\n\\nEstablish the view from evidence: group a call by `USAGE_ACCOUNT_ID` (Step 5.1). A region-restriction IAM policy (`aws:RequestedRegion` deny) on the\\nagent\\'s role must exempt this service, or the calls will fail.\\n\\n### 6. `GroupBy` supports at most the three listed dimensions\\n\\n`USAGE_ACCOUNT_ID`, `REGION`, `SERVICE`. There is **no** resource-level or tag-level\\ngrouping. Global services such as CloudFront are reported under the\\nRegion \"Global\".\\n\\n## GetEstimatedWaterAllocation\\n\\n**Reporting only.** Water exists so a customer can cite an AWS-sourced figure in their own\\ndisclosure (the definitions align with the\\n[CDP water accounting note](https://cdn.cdp.net/cdp-production/cms/guidance_docs/pdfs/000/001/561/original/CDP-technical-note-water-accounting-definitions.pdf)\\nand [GRI 303:2018](https://globalreporting.org/pdf.ashx?id=12488), which is what makes it\\nusable there). The console limits how many records it displays; the API and Data Exports return the full history | Back to 2023, published annually: year Y in Q2 of Y+1 (2025 data in Q2 2026); current year absent |\\n\\nThe same half-open rule applies, on years: year `Y` is returned iff\\n`Start <= Y-01-01T00:00:00Z < End`.\\n\\nGranularity is the one asymmetry that errors loudly rather than silently \u2014 `MONTHLY`,\\n`QUARTERLY_CALENDAR`, `YEARLY_FISCAL` and `QUARTERLY_FISCAL` all return\\n`ValidationException: Invalid input: invalid granularity: only YEARLY_CALENDAR can be requested`.\\nOmitting `Granularity` entirely also works and yields annual results.\\n\\nThe genuine silent trap is the range. The docs say: \"If requesting partial time periods, data\\nwill be returned based on the smallest supported granularity. For example, requesting\\n`2025-04-01T00:00:00Z` to `2026-04-01T00:00:00Z` with `YEARLY_CALENDAR` will return all the\\ndata for 2026 only.\" **Live, that request returns zero results** \u2014 the range contains\\n`2026-01-01` but 2026 has no published water data yet, and 2025 is excluded because the range\\ndoes not contain `2025-01-01`. Either way the lesson holds and is stronger than the docs\\nsuggest: a range that looks like 12 months can return the wrong year *or nothing at all*.\\nAlways send a January 1st `Start` and read the `TimePeriod` on every result.\\n\\n### Two things to state whenever you report the figure\\n\\n> \"The methodology allocates total water withdrawal from AWS data center operations to\\n> individual customer accounts based on their proportional cloud service usage. Total water\\n> withdrawal is defined as the total volume of water taken from any source ... regardless of\\n> whether it is eventually returned to the environment.\"\\n\\n1. **Withdrawal, not consumption.** Water returned to the environment still counts. Calling\\n   it water \"used up\" or \"consumed\" is a different metric and overstates impact.\\n2. **Data center operations only.** Water embodied in upstream electricity generation is\\n   excluded, and for most grids that is the larger share. Without this caveat the customer\\n   reads the number as a total water footprint.\\n\\nSame top-down allocation as carbon, so the same non-attributability caveats apply in full.\\n\\n## Methodology Background\\n\\n### Top-down allocation\\n\\nCCFT does not meter each customer\\'s energy consumption. AWS computes total infrastructure\\nemissions, then allocates a share to each customer based on proportional usage, flowing\\nthrough cluster \u2192 rack \u2192 service \u2192 account.\\n\\nTwo consequences that customers find counter-intuitive, and that the skill must be able\\nto explain:\\n\\n1. **Your allocated share can change because other customers\\' usage changed**, with no\\n   change on your side.\\n2. **AWS-side improvements reduce your reported emissions with no action from you** \u2014\\n   hardware refresh, PUE improvements, additional renewable procurement.\\n\\nBoth mean reported emissions are not a clean feedback signal for your architecture work.\\n\\n### Methodology changes\\n\\nThe model version is revisioned (`v3.0.1` observed live for carbon; the user guide documents\\nthe `v3.0.x` line). A revision can move reported figures substantially with **zero** change in\\nusage. Report the version the API actually returns \u2014 never a version quoted from documentation.\\n\\n**The API always restates history under the current model.** Per the\\n[`EstimatedCarbonEmissions`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sustainability/latest/APIReference/API_EstimatedCarbonEmissions.html)\\ndocs:\\n\\n> \"The AWS Sustainability service reflects the most recent model version for every month.\\n> You will not see two entries for the same month with different `ModelVersion` values.\"\\n\\nTwo consequences, and they are the opposite of what you might expect:\\n\\n1. **You cannot detect a methodology change from this API.** Every month in a single\\n   response carries the same `ModelVersion`, so a cross-period comparison of `ModelVersion`\\n   will never differ. {"id": "a72b87ab-c6bb-4bb5-8093-1f2ed8a6502c", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Short answer: no, your footprint didn't regress — the number moved because AWS revised its carbon methodology, not because your workload changed. And no, there's no way to re-pull the old figure through the API; the 412.7 you already have *is* that figure.

**Why the number is different**

The Sustainability API always restates history under whichever model version is current — it never returns two values for the same month under two different versions. Today's call shows `ModelVersion v3.0.1` on all twelve months of 2025, which means AWS has recalculated your entire Jan–Dec 2025 footprint under v3.0.1. Your original 412.7 MTCO2e was captured under an earlier version, before that revision happened. So you're not comparing "last year" to "this year" — you're comparing the same twelve months under two different measurement instruments. A methodology revision can move the reported number substantially with zero change in actual usage, which lines up exactly with "we did no optimization work" on your side.

**Did your footprint regress?**

No. Before attributing any change in reported emissions to the workload, the standard approach is to rule out non-architecture causes in order — comparison validity, methodology version, grid carbon intensity, AWS-side infrastructure changes (hardware refresh, PUE, renewable procurement), and allocation-share shifts — before even considering actual usage. In your case the methodology-version mismatch alone fully accounts for it: you told me the old figure came from an earlier model, and the new pull is uniformly v3.0.1. There's no need to go further down that list. A 468.3 vs 412.7 delta under these conditions is the instrument changing, not the infrastructure.

**Can I pull the figure under the old model?**

Not through `GetEstimatedCarbonEmissions` — that's the key limitation here. The API only ever serves the current model version; it has no way to return a historical model's value for a month that's since been restated. The only path to old-model figures is AWS Data Exports (CSV/Parquet, partitioned by `model_version`), and that only works if the export was **set up before the revision landed** — it can't retroactively recover a superseded version. Since you captured 412.7 at the time it was current, that number already **is** your old-model figure; there's no third, independently-retrievable copy of it sitting anywhere in AWS's systems today.

If you want to be able to track methodology changes going forward (so a future revision doesn't leave you without the prior figure), I'd recommend setting up a Data Export now — that's the only mechanism that preserves old `model_version` data across revisions.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
